title: Code of conduct
text: The MIG journal club is a place to read carefully and disagree well. These expectations apply to meetings, to this repository, and to anything published here.

title: Code of conduct
text:
Expected behaviour

Criticise work, not people. “This design cannot separate cells from donors” is useful. “The authors clearly don’t understand single-cell data” is not.
Assume good faith. Papers are written under constraints we cannot see, by people who are not present to reply.
Make space. Journal clubs are dominated by whoever is most confident. Presenters and chairs should actively invite quieter attendees in.
Ask the naive question. If you are lost, others are too, and saying so improves the discussion for everyone.

title: Code of conduct
text:
Publication and attribution
Meetings are reported and published on this public site. Because of that:

Reports name the presenter, and may name people who proposed follow-up reading. Discussion points are otherwise attributed impersonally.
You can ask not to be named. Tell the organisers, before or after the meeting, and we will remove the attribution. No reason needed.
Criticism published here is directed at the work. Before a report is merged it is reviewed by someone other than its author, partly to check this.

See contributing for the full reporting process.

title: Code of conduct
text:
Unacceptable behaviour
Harassment, discrimination, personal attacks, and dismissive remarks about someone’s background or level of experience are not tolerated, in meetings or in this repository.

title: Code of conduct
text:
Reporting
Raise a concern with the journal club organisers directly. Anything involving the conduct of an organiser can be taken to the University of Melbourne’s staff complaint channels.

title: MIG Journal Club
text: We meet to read one or more papers closely. Each meeting is summarised here: what the paper claimed, what we discussed, what stayed unresolved, and what we might read next. New members and visitors are welcome.

title: MIG Journal Club
text: Past meetings

title: Causal inference starts with the question
text:
Papers. Swales J. The troublesome search for evidence: three cultures in need of integration. Journal of the Royal Society of Medicine 93(8):402–407 (2000). doi:10.1177/014107680009300804
Lu H, Li F, Lesko CR, Fink DS, Rudolph KE, Harhay MO, Rentsch CT, Fiellin DA, Gonsalves GS. Four targets: an enhanced framework for guiding causal inference from observational data. International Journal of Epidemiology 54(1):dyaf003 (2025). doi:10.1093/ije/dyaf003
Dickerman BA, García-Albéniz X, Logan RW, Denaxas S, Hernán MA. Avoidable flaws in observational analyses: an application to statins and cancer. Nature Medicine 25(10):1601–1606 (2019). doi:10.1038/s41591-019-0597-x
Presented by Jiadong Mao · 1 September 2026 · Slides

title: Causal inference starts with the question
section: The question comes before the method
text:
The question comes before the method
Together, the three papers make a case for treating causal inference first as a discipline of question-setting. A causal question must say what intervention is being compared with what alternative, for whom, over what period, and against which outcome. Choosing a model before settling those points does not merely leave details unspecified; it can change the question being answered.
Dickerman and colleagues provide the sharpest demonstration. Using electronic health records from 733,804 UK adults, they compared statin initiation with no initiation. An analysis that classified people by whether they accumulated more than four years of statin use produced a hazard ratio of 0.22 for total cancer, suggesting a very large protective association. The classification used future information: to enter the long-term-user group, a person had to remain alive, cancer-free and under follow-up long enough to accumulate that exposure. This created immortal time bias.
When eligibility, treatment assignment and the start of follow-up were aligned at time zero to emulate a target trial, the corresponding intention-to-treat hazard ratio was 1.02. The same flaw reversed the apparent direction of the association with type 2 diabetes: defining exposure by observed duration gave a hazard ratio of 0.20, whereas the target-trial estimate was 1.11. The lesson is not that observational data cannot support causal inference. It is that a large dataset and a sophisticated analysis cannot repair a comparison defined using information that would have been unavailable when treatment was assigned.

title: Causal inference starts with the question
section: Four targets expose what the estimate means
text:
Four targets expose what the estimate means
Lu and colleagues proposed four targets for causal inference on observation data. The target estimand states the treatment effect of interest, including the intervention, comparator, outcome and follow-up. The target population states to whom the answer is intended to apply. The target trial is the hypothetical pragmatic randomised trial the observational analysis seeks to emulate. Target validity then asks whether the estimate is valid for that estimand and population, combining the usual concerns about internal and external validity.
This framework shifts difficult conversations to the beginning of a study. “Do statins prevent cancer?” is not yet a complete causal question: initiation and sustained treatment are different interventions, dose and adherence require definitions, and the relevant population and follow-up period must be fixed. Changing these choices after seeing the result changes the estimand and invites cherry-picking.
The discussion connected these targets to three identification assumptions. Consistency requires the intervention and outcome to be defined well enough that an observed treatment corresponds to the treatment being analysed. Positivity requires both treatment strategies to be possible for every relevant kind of participant. Exchangeability requires the comparison groups not to differ, after conditioning on measured information, in other causes of the outcome. Health-seeking behaviour illustrates the last problem: people who take preventive medication may also seek care, undergo screening or change behaviour in ways that affect their cancer risk.
Making assumptions explicit is useful, but does not make them true. An analysis can therefore supply a causal answer only conditional on assumptions that data alone may not verify. Disagreement about a causal conclusion may persist because attendees accept different assumptions, rather than because one side has chosen the wrong estimator.

title: Causal inference starts with the question
section: Cell experiments intervene, but design still sets the claim
text:
Cell experiments intervene, but design still sets the claim
The same reasoning applies to single-cell experiments without requiring every study to adopt the machinery of observational epidemiology. A pathway-inhibition experiment can specify an intervention, a matched control, an outcome at a fixed time and a target population of donors. In that sense, experimental biologists already reason causally whenever they perturb a system and compare outcomes.
The causal framing nevertheless reveals familiar failure modes. Cells are not independent biological replicates when treatment is assigned at the donor or culture level. Quality-control filtering can also become post-treatment selection: if an intervention changes RNA abundance or cell viability, applying the same threshold may selectively remove the cells most affected by treatment. Finally, a result across a small set of donors does not automatically transport to the population the biological claim names.
One unresolved point was whether formal causal inference is necessary for useful biological or clinical work. Yeganeh Khazaei argued that action can be justified by a sufficiently strong body of evidence without every study establishing a causal effect in isolation. Others stressed that discovery experiments often leave the question flexible and use a later perturbation as validation, which does not necessarily reproduce a pre-specified target trial. Jiadong’s proposed middle ground was causal inference as an attitude to design: ask what would have to be compared, make the assumptions visible, and state how far the resulting claim can travel.

title: Causal inference starts with the question
section: Evidence does not come from one culture
text:
Evidence does not come from one culture
Swales’ three “cultures” supplied a broader account of evidence: mechanistic biomedicine asks whether an intervention could work, clinical experience asks how it behaves in whole patients, and numerical evidence estimates whether it does work across groups. Each can correct the others. Homeopathy has had apparently favourable numerical results without a credible mechanism or clinical acceptance. Conversely, suppressing ventricular arrhythmias after myocardial infarction had mechanistic and clinical plausibility, yet randomised evidence showed that particular antiarrhythmic drugs increased mortality.
The biological analogue of clinical evidence remained unsettled. For cell and animal studies it might include accumulated domain knowledge about the model, the experimental design and the conditions under which results have previously translated. It would not replace direct evidence in patients, but it still constrains which causal accounts are plausible. No resolution was reached on how the three cultures should be weighted, or on what their precise analogues are outside clinical medicine.
Meta-analysis does not remove this design problem. Pooling studies that define exposure, time zero or eligible populations incompatibly can make a biased answer more precise. Yeganeh noted that when clinical studies are highly heterogeneous, a systematic or scoping review may be more defensible than forcing a pooled estimate. Inclusion criteria and the target question must therefore be settled before synthesis, just as they must be settled before modelling a single cohort.

title: Causal inference starts with the question
text:
Follow-up reading
Yeganeh proposed adaptive platform trials as a practical extension to the discussion. These trials use a master protocol to evaluate several interventions and can add or drop arms under pre-specified decision rules. A general entry point is Angus DC, Alexander BM, Berry S, et al. Adaptive platform trials: definition, design, conduct and reporting considerations. Nature Reviews Drug Discovery 18:797–807 (2019). doi:10.1038/s41573-019-0034-3

title: Pre-training scale in single-cell foundation models
text:
Paper. DenAdel A, Hughes M, Thoutam A, Gupta A, Navia AW, Fusi N, Raghavan S, Winter PS, Amini AP, Crawford L. Evaluating the role of pre-training dataset size and diversity on single-cell foundation model performance. Nature Methods (2026). doi:10.1038/s41592-026-03120-y
Presented by David Hirst · 18 August 2026

title: Pre-training scale in single-cell foundation models
text:
The study
The paper asks whether single-cell foundation models (scFMs) obey the scaling behaviour established for language models. The authors subsampled the 22.2 million-cell scTab corpus (164 cell types, 5,052 donors, 56 tissues, drawn from the CELLxGENE census) at 1, 10, 25, 50 and 75%, under three sampling schemes — uniform, cell-type re-weighted, and geometric sketching — and pre-trained five architectures of increasing complexity on each: PCA, scVI, a masked autoencoder (SSL), Geneformer, and SCimilarity. This yields 400 pre-trained models and 6,400 downstream evaluations spanning zero-shot and fine-tuned cell-type classification, batch integration, and perturbation response prediction.
Performance saturates at roughly 1% of the corpus, approximately 200,000 cells and under a gigabyte of counts. Diversity-enriched sampling confers no advantage over uniform sampling. In every task, the pre-trained models are matched or beaten by unsupervised PCA computed directly on the evaluation dataset and by logistic regression on highly variable genes.

title: Pre-training scale in single-cell foundation models
text:
Terminology clarified in discussion
Two terms were first discussed, both used loosely in the literature. Foundation model was initially equated with large language model, but the paper adopts the broader sense of any model whose learned representation is reused as a scaffold for downstream tasks — which is why a pre-trained PCA qualifies. Every architecture here is used identically: it supplies a low-dimensional embedding (loading vectors for PCA, encoder weights for scVI), and that embedding is transferred to the new dataset. Zero-shot denotes use of the embedding without further training, with classification performed by nearest neighbours; fine-tuned denotes retraining of some or all parameters, which for PCA means fixing the loadings and appending a neural network classifier.
Jiadong proposed a reframing of the plateau in terms of effective sample size. In single-cell data the effective sample size lies between the number of donors and the number of cells. Pseudo-bulking sits at the conservative extreme: it guarantees independence but discards within-donor variation. On this reading the saturation point is an empirical estimate of where the effective sample size sits for a given learning task — the authors did not explain this.

title: Pre-training scale in single-cell foundation models
text:
Criticisms
The dominant concern was that the study varies cells rather than donors. Sample size in this context means biological replication; 5,052 donors is adequate for biological inference and far short of what a large model requires. Downsampling cells within a fixed corpus therefore adds repetition and technical noise rather than information, and the observed plateau may say more about scTab than about scFMs. Rerunning the design on an independent pre-training corpus, or subsampling studies rather than cells, would separate the two.
Related to this, several attendees argued that the value of a foundation model should be assessed against deliberately heterogeneous, noisy training data. The study considered the training on a corpus assembled under (potentially) broadly uniform protocols.
The provenance of the ground-truth cell-type labels was raised and remains unresolved. Public atlas annotations are routinely generated by PCA followed by clustering and manual labelling. If the reference labels were produced this way, a PCA-derived classifier recovering them is close to circular, and the headline result that simple baselines win loses much of its force. It was also noted that PCA is the current practical default rather than an optimal reduction, and that cell-type-discriminating variance can fall outside the retained components.
On evaluation design, fine-tuning splits a single dataset 80/10/10 and reports test performance from the same study, which inflates accuracy relative to the realistic case of training and testing on independent studies. In fairness, the authors did guard against leakage at the corpus level by restricting evaluation datasets to studies published after the 2023-05-15 census release, so none appear in scTab; the objection applies to the fine-tuning split alone.
The choice of downstream tasks drew the sharpest criticism. Cell-type annotation and batch correction are largely solved problems, so demonstrating that foundation models fail to improve on them is a weak test of the paradigm. The question left standing is what a general-purpose scFM is actually for: if the only tasks that generalise across studies are ones already handled by conventional methods, the biologically interesting questions may be irreducibly study-specific.
Perturbation response prediction supports that reading. For three of the four compounds tested, every fine-tuned model was outperformed by a baseline predicting no change in expression. Discussion attributed this partly to uncharacterised technical effects in the underlying data, and noted that this is precisely the regime in which robust linear methods should be expected to win.
The absence of pre-training learning curves was noted as a gap. A study framed around dataset size and generalisation should report training and validation loss as a function of corpus size and show where the two diverge; the reported downstream F1 curves are only indirect evidence.

title: Pre-training scale in single-cell foundation models
section: Transfer works for language but maybe not for expression?
text:
Transfer works for language but maybe not for expression?
The most developed technical argument concerned batch effects. In natural language, batch effects are enumerable — regional variants differ in orthography, idiom and lexical choice — so a sufficiently large corpus contains them all and the model learns to marginalise over them. Transcriptomic batch effects are not enumerable: each operator, day and reagent lot generates a novel effect, so no corpus contains the full space. A review by Shihua Zhang’s team was cited as making this argument. A complementary point was raised on target complexity: token combinatorics in language are effectively unbounded, whereas cell-type space is small, and separate ongoing work indicates that roughly 150 features suffice for cell-type prediction. Most genes contribute nothing to the task, so additional data and features dilute rather than sharpen the signal.
Three constructive directions followed: importing the statistical genetics toolkit (GWAS, fine-mapping, causal inference) rather than relying on scale alone; aligning the pre-training objective with the intended downstream task, for which the paper supplies direct evidence in SCimilarity’s contrastive objective and its correspondingly strong cell-type performance; and moving toward automated experimental design rather than passive accumulation of data.

title: Pre-training scale in single-cell foundation models
text:
Follow-up reading
Chengyi proposed a companion paper: Rosen Y, Roohani Y, Agrawal A, Samotorčan L, Tabula Sapiens Consortium, Quake SR, Leskovec J. Universal cell embedding provides a foundation model for cell biology. Nature 656:183–191 (2026). doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10689-z
UCE pursues the same premise — self-supervised pre-training on a large corpus to yield a universal per-cell embedding — but reports strong zero-shot downstream performance without fine-tuning, across 36 million cells and over 1,000 cell types, including generalisation to species absent from training. The apparent contradiction with DenAdel et al. is the reason to read the two together, and turns on evaluation task, corpus composition, and whether the reported gains survive a PCA baseline.

title: About
text:
The MIG journal club is run by Melbourne Integrative Genomics at the University of Melbourne. We read one paper — occasionally a small set — and discuss it properly for an hour.
Papers are chosen mainly by whoever is presenting. We will also discuss towards the end of each session what papers the audience what to see. Example topics include (not limited to):

title: About
text:
When we meet
Monthly, on a Thursday at 3:30 pm, in Room 124, Building 184. See the next meeting for the current date.

title: About
text:
How to join
Anyone interested is welcome — MIG members, people elsewhere at the University and affiliated institutes, visitors. There is no membership and no commitment to attend regularly.
To be added to the meeting invitations, contact Jiadong Mao.

title: About
section: Do I need to read the paper before the session?
text:
Do I need to read the paper before the session?
You are welcome to come without having read the paper. Most people have skimmed it; a few have read it closely; the discussion is built to work either way.

title: About
section: How meetings are recorded and published
text:
How meetings are recorded and published
Meetings are audio-recorded for edited transcripts to be published. Please read this section before your first meeting.

The recording is used only to compile the report, and the recording itself is not published.
Reports name the presenter, and may name people who proposed follow-up reading. Other contributions are attributed anonymously — “it was noted”, “one attendee argued” — because room microphones do not always separate speakers reliably.
Every report is reviewed by someone other than its author before it is published. That review checks the science, and also checks that criticism is aimed at the work rather than at the people who did it.
You can ask not to be named, before or after a meeting, with no reason needed. Tell an organiser and the attribution is removed. (You can also pick a pseudonym, say Socrates.)

Discussion here is often critical, sometimes sharply. That is the point of a journal club. It is published in the spirit of open scientific disagreement, and we try hard to keep it directed at the work. If you are an author of something we have discussed and feel we have got you wrong, open an issue — we will correct it, and you are very welcome to reply.

title: About
text:
Presenting
Presenting is informal: pick a paper you want to think about, bring it, and lead the discussion. You do not need slides, although slides are recommended. See contributing if you would like to report on your own session, or propose a paper for someone else to present.

title: Contributing
text: There are three ways to contribute, in increasing order of effort.

title: Contributing
text:
1. Fix something — one click
Every page has an “Edit this page” link in the right-hand margin. Click it and GitHub opens an editor, forks the repository for you, and offers to open a pull request. You do not need to install anything, or know git.
Use it for typos, broken links, a mangled citation, or a point we recorded wrong. Small corrections are genuinely welcome — nobody will think less of a one-word PR.

title: Contributing
text:
2. Propose a paper
Open a paper proposal. You do not have to present it yourself.

title: Contributing
text:
3. Report about the meeting
Reports are usually drafted from the recording by an organiser and then reviewed by the presenter. If you would rather write your own, do that — it is better.

The process

Copy _template/ to posts/YYYY-MM-DD-short-slug/ and rename it. The date prefix is a filing convention; the date: field in the front matter is what actually orders the site, so keep the two in sync.
Write the report in index.qmd, filling in the front matter (author stays empty — see below).
Open a pull request. The PR template has a short checklist — it exists to catch the two things that actually cause problems, copyright and attribution.
A second person reviews and merges. Never merge your own report. The reviewer checks the science, and checks that criticism reads as being about the work rather than the people.

To preview locally you need Quarto:
quarto preview
This is optional. Reports are prose, so the GitHub pull request diff is perfectly readable on its own, and CI renders every PR to catch broken YAML.


Front matter
Every field is already in _template/index.qmd — copy the template and fill it in, rather than typing the block out from memory. Three fields take judgement:

title — short and descriptive, naming the topic. Not the paper’s title.
description — one line. It appears in the listing, in link previews when someone pastes the URL into Teams or email, and in the feed, so it has to work on its own. Say what the paper claims, then the question the discussion left open.
author — leave it empty. Reports are summaries compiled from a recording, not authored pieces. Naming the presenter here would credit them with writing something they did not write.

draft: true hides the report from the listing while you work. Remove it when ready. Note the page still renders — blank — at its final URL while drafting.
Once a report is merged, do not rename its folder. The URL is the permanent address people cite and link to.


Categories
Pick from this list, so the sidebar stays usable:
single-cell · spatial · multi-omics · microbiome · genomics · statistics · causal-inference · experimental-design · batch-effects · machine-learning · foundation-models · benchmarking · reproducibility · meta-science
Two or three per report is plenty. To add a new category, propose it in your PR — the point of a fixed list is that scRNA-seq, scRNAseq and single-cell RNA-seq don’t become three separate entries.

title: Contributing
text:
Figures and copyright
This is a public repository, so this part matters.

Never commit a PDF of a paper. Link to the DOI.
Do not screenshot figures from paywalled papers. Reproducing a figure from a closed-access paper on a public website is a copyright breach.

A figure in a report must be one of:

Your own — a schematic you drew, or a plot you made from public data.
From an open-access paper under a CC licence, reproduced with attribution and a link to the source. Check the licence; “free to read” is not the same as “free to reuse”.
Absent. Describing a figure in prose is almost always enough, and it is what most of our reports do.

Short quotations from a paper are fine, in quotation marks, with a citation.

title: Contributing
text:
Writing style
The house style is narrative prose, not bullet-point minutes. What we are trying to capture is the argument — the objection someone raised, why it mattered, and whether it survived. A reader who did not attend should be able to follow the reasoning.

Sections follow the shape of the discussion, not a fixed template.
Name the presenter and anyone who proposed follow-up reading. Attribute other points impersonally: room microphones do not separate speakers reliably, and people speak more freely knowing that.
Criticise the work, not the authors. See the code of conduct.
Record disagreement that was left unresolved. It is more useful than a tidy consensus that nobody actually reached.
If the discussion relied on unpublished or in-progress work by someone who attended, check with them before it goes on a public site.

Do not put internal notes in <!-- HTML comments -->. They are passed straight through into the published page source. Use a ::: {.content-hidden} div instead.
The first report is a reasonable model.
